group.passage: Every day, people cross busy streets on black-and-white stripes without thinking twice. Text A explains how the pedestrian crossing came about, and in Text B, a traffic police officer talks about how to cross the street safely.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: From Stones to Stripes
passage_parts.text: Walkers needed help to cross the street long before there were cars. In the old Roman town of Pompeii, dirty water often ran down the roads. To keep their feet dry, people crossed on large stones set in a line from one side to the other. Modern crossings began in Britain. By the early 1930s, cars had become common, and thousands of people were killed on the roads every year. In 1934, the government chose special places where walkers could cross. Rows of metal studs were set into the road there, and a black-and-white pole with an orange globe on top stood at each end. Over the years, however, drivers began to pay less attention to the crossings, and the studs were not easy to see. So in 1951, the studs were removed, and the government decided to paint wide black-and-white stripes across the road. Because the stripes looked like the coat of a zebra, people soon began calling it a “zebra crossing.”

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Ask an Officer
passage_parts.text: Officer Lin has directed traffic near schools for many years. When we asked about the most common mistake that walkers make, she did not need to think. “Too many people look at their phones while they cross,” she said. “Keep your phone in your pocket until you reach the other side.” She also warned that a zebra crossing is not always safe. “Those black-and-white stripes tell drivers to stop, but some drivers are in a hurry, and others simply don’t see you. Before you step out, check both ways and wait until the cars have stopped.” At night, she added, walkers should wear something bright. Dark clothes are hard for drivers to see after sunset. Her advice for drivers was simple: slow down whenever there is a crossing ahead, especially near schools. “Children are small, and they may suddenly run out between parked cars.”

translation_zh.text:
【引言】每天，人們走在黑白條紋上穿越繁忙的街道，連想都不用想。Text A 說明行人穿越道是怎麼來的；Text B 是一位交通警察談怎麼安全地過馬路。
【A 從石頭到條紋】早在汽車出現以前，行人過馬路就需要幫忙了。在古羅馬城鎮龐貝，髒水常常沿著道路流下。為了不弄濕雙腳，人們踩著從路的一邊排到另一邊的大石頭過街。現代的行人穿越道始於英國。到了 1930 年代初，汽車已經很普遍，每年都有好幾千人死於道路上。1934 年，政府選定了一些行人可以穿越的特定地點：那裡的路面嵌入一排排金屬圓釘，兩端各立著一根黑白相間的柱子，柱頂有一顆橘色圓球。然而，隨著時間過去，駕駛越來越不注意這些穿越道，那些圓釘也不容易看見。所以在 1951 年，圓釘被拆除，政府決定在路面上漆上寬寬的黑白條紋。因為條紋看起來像斑馬身上的毛色，人們很快就開始叫它「斑馬線」。
【B 請教警官】林警官在學校附近指揮交通已經很多年了。我們問她行人最常犯的錯誤是什麼，她想都不用想。「太多人過馬路時還在看手機，」她說，「把手機放在口袋裡，等走到對面再拿出來。」她也提醒，斑馬線不一定安全。「那些黑白條紋是告訴駕駛要停車，但有些駕駛在趕時間，有些則根本沒看到你。踏出去之前，先看清楚兩邊，等車子都停下來再走。」她補充說，晚上行人應該穿顏色鮮亮的衣服，深色衣服在日落後很難被駕駛看見。她給駕駛的建議很簡單：只要前方有穿越道就要減速，尤其是在學校附近。「孩子個子小，可能會突然從停著的車子之間衝出來。」

problems: Text A「So in 1951, the studs were removed, and the government decided to paint wide black-and-white stripes across the road.」的「圓釘被拆除」事實單沒有依據（f6 只說 1949 年試驗新標線、f7 只說 1951 年核准黑白條紋加兩側燈標），而且與史實不符：1951 年的新規定是在原本用圓釘標示的穿越道上加漆黑白條紋，圓釘保留下來標示穿越道的範圍（Commercial Motor 1951-07-13 報導新規定保留圓釘；英國其後的 zebra crossing 規章到現行 1997 年規章仍有 studs 條款）。選文把「圓釘看不清楚→拆掉圓釘→改漆條紋」寫成因果，是錯誤的史實，要改選文（例如 stripes were painted between the rows of studs），第 3 題 D、E 的解析也要跟著改
